title: To be clear, I don’t review shows in preview anymore, but that’s beca...
transcript: let's talk about Broadway previews because the discourse is flaring up again and it's funny because I've almost made this exact video like 10 times in the last couple of years but I keep chickening out because like I do have strong feelings on it but I'm also a little bit afraid to wade into this topic because it's sensitive and tricky and nuanced I don't claim to have the one right answer but here's where I'm at on this first of all I do think if you're reacting publicly to a preview performance that should absolutely impact how you talk about it both in terms of making it clear that you saw a preview and also not critiquing things that are subject to change But that leads me to kind of my main point that I wanna discuss here which is this question of what is likely to change during previews? and how much will that sway your reaction? I think some of the disconnect in this debate is that a lot of the pushback is coming from artists and sure if you're an artist in the middle of the preview process you're getting pages and pages of new material, new numbers, in rehearsals during the day, and just generally getting more settled in the show you have this tangible sense of how much the show is changing because you can measure it in your own hard work that experience isn't wrong but I do question if it aligns with if it reflects how audiences seeing it for the first time are actually experiencing it even if there's undeniably a huge volume a huge quantity of changes I think there's still this question of is it changing in the ways that it needs to? is it changing to the extent that it needs to? and sometimes is it changing at the foundational level that it needs to to meaningfully sway audience reactions? because in my anecdotal experience I get the sense that the things that really make or break my opinion of the show are generally not the things that are likely to change during previews it seems like nowadays once the show is in previews there is a certain critical mass of work that has already taken place a foundation that the show is built on that would take more than a few weeks of previews to change assuming they even would if they could which is not always a given and I get the sense again, in just my anecdotal observation that the overarching word of mouth in previews vs. after opening are not substantially different from each other and absolutely there are exceptions I think Shuffle Along is a great example of a show where the word of mouth drastically changed during previews but in another sense they're also kind of the exception that proves the rule because they took a hiatus to do massive rewrites they cut like 30 minutes worth of material some of which was good material but they still cut it to serve the overall show they even laid off one of the principal actors because they cut her role the turnaround in their word of mouth was the direct result of some pretty extreme measures I do think the natural counter-argument to what I'm saying is like can't we give the shows space to become these exceptions? even if it's rare let's give them the chance? and I don't know, maybe maybe we should but it's a tough ask when audiences have been trained to expect that that won't happen in the meantime, prospective audience members want to know what they can expect from a show that has opened itself up for public viewing
